note: Organises evaluation into what, where and how, which is a workable skeleton for the testing section of an audit programme.
title: A Survey on Evaluation of Large Language Models
journal: ACM Transactions on Intelligent Systems and Technology

reading.body:
A 2023 survey of how large language models are tested has drawn 3,810 citations, which makes it the reference point for evaluation practice rather than a single method.

The survey sorts evaluation into three questions: what is being tested, in what setting, and with which techniques and test sets. That structure spans general language work, reasoning, medicine, ethics, education, science, social science, and agent use, and it records both successes and failures. The authors argue evaluation should be treated as a field in its own right, because better testing produces better models and a clearer view of social risk.

For AI specifically, the useful claim is that capability is only meaningful once something measures it. A model that scores well on one test set and fails on another has not been shown to be capable, only shown to be measured. The survey's breadth across domains is the evidence for that: the same class of system is assessed differently in medicine than in reasoning, and the results do not transfer automatically.

The data does not say which benchmarks are best, how any specific model scored, or how evaluation should be funded and staffed. It is a survey with a high citation count, not a result. Nothing here speaks to compute, data centers, or power, and the reader should not read the citation count as a measure of the survey's accuracy.

explain_beginner: This paper reviews ways to test large language models. It groups testing around three questions: what abilities or areas to check, in what situations or uses, and with which techniques and test sets. It covers many areas such as general language tasks, reasoning, medicine, ethics, education, science, social science, and agent uses. It also collects examples where models did well and where they failed. The authors argue testing should be a serious field of its own, because better testing helps build better models and understand risks to society. Open problems remain.
explain_business: This paper reviews how large language models are tested. It groups testing into what should be checked, in which settings, and with which techniques and test sets. It covers many uses, from language and reasoning to healthcare, ethics, education, science, and agents. It notes both successes and failures. For leaders, the practical message is that model evaluation should be planned as an ongoing discipline, not a one time check. That informs decisions about where models are used, how their risks are understood, and how evaluation supports development. Remaining difficulties exist.
explain_practitioner: This survey reviews how large language models are evaluated. It sorts the field into three questions: which abilities or domains are tested, in which situations testing happens, and which techniques and test sets are used. It covers broad language work, reasoning, healthcare, moral questions, learning, physical and social sciences, and tool using agents. It reports both successful and unsuccessful cases across tasks. The key result is a call to treat evaluation as a central discipline that supports better model development. The authors also identify remaining difficulties and keep related open source materials available.
